transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-05-11
- Time: 14:30 PT
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Aria, Liam, Priya, Samir (BlueEcho)

Auto Summary (automated):
- Intro/partner framing: BlueEcho wants to integrate Redwood via an "Orbit Connector" offering — sell as channel onramp into their cloud managed GPU offering; explore technical feasibility and SLA mapping.
- Key concerns: network/VPC peering, tenancy (shared vs dedicated), KMS/encryption, and GPU SKU parity (H100/A100) plus NVLink for large-context models.
- Next: share spec + schedule SE deep dive and preliminary benchmarking.

Topics discussed:
- BlueEcho partner program + go-to-market model
- Integration patterns (API proxy vs direct private peering)
- Security/compliance: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
- Performance: latency targets, batching, KV cache, multi-GPU model sharding
- Commercial & pilot scope

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya, I'm the AE, with Carlos our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Aria (BlueEcho): Good, thanks Maya. Excited to chat — I put Priya and Liam on, and Samir will join after his 2:30.
[00:12] Priya (BlueEcho): Hi all.
[00:13] Carlos (Redwood): Quick technical hail, we'll keep this high-level then drill where you want.
[00:18] Liam (BlueEcho): Sounds good. We wanted to make sure we cover the Orbit connector idea, especially what networking patterns you support — private peering, VPC, reverse-proxy, etc.
[00:28] Maya: Yep. At a high level Redwood supports hosted API, dedicated pools, and private deployments. For partner onramps we typically do either a direct VPC peering + private endpoint or a connector model where partner hosts an adaptor that routes requests into Redwood's control plane with an mTLS connection.
[00:40] Aria: When you say "connector" is that something we run in our network or you provide?
[00:44] Carlos: It can be either. Most partners prefer a lightweight adaptor that runs in their tenancy — it's basically a small service that handles auth, routing and optionally batching before forwarding to the Redwood serving runtime. That minimizes egress and keeps keys KMS-protected on your side.
[00:55] Liam: Ok that matters — our customers require keys to never leave their VPC/AWS KMS. Is it possible to do that with your adaptor?
[01:02] Carlos: Yes — the adaptor can be configured to sign requests locally and we support customer-managed keys for encryption at rest. For private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM and audit logs remain in your account. For hosted or dedicated we have bring-your-own-key (BYOK) options too.
[01:15] Aria: Great. Can you talk about model placement? We run a mix of H100 and A100 fleets across regions; need to know if Redwood can route by SKU and fall back to lower-cost instances when needed.
[01:24] Maya: Absolutely. Redwood has smart routing policies — you can pin SKUs or model variants, and define fallback tiers. Our runtime can also select quantized variants for cost-sensitive paths. Carlos, do you want to add?
[01:33] Carlos: Sure. On the serving side we expose routing by tags — you can tag instances as h100-us-central, a100-eu-west etc. The control plane maps requests to those tags, and if capacity isn't there we can failover to a compatible quantized model. We also surface per-token cost and latency metrics so you can tune policies.
[01:48] Priya: That sounds nice. On the commercial side Aria and I are thinking of two paths: reseller model or a co-sell where BlueEcho bundles Redwood as a managed onramp. We'll need pricing guardrails and SLAs.
[02:00] Maya: Totally — we can propose both. For reseller we have partner discounts and a usage reporting API; for co-sell we can offer joint pricing with reserved capacity for your customers. We'll follow up with a partner commercial template.
[02:10] Liam: Technical Q: what's the expected latency hit if we do a connector that does batching on the partner side vs pure direct low-latency path? Our workloads include interactive chat where P95 matter.
[02:20] Carlos: Batching reduces per-token cost but can add tail latency. Our runtime supports continuous batching and smart batching thresholds. If you need strict P95 under 300ms we recommend direct private peering with small-batch/streaming enabled and prefix KV cache turned on — that reduces token generation time. If throughput is the priority you can batch bigger at ~50-100ms windows.
[02:39] Liam: Hmm ok, do you support streaming responses through the connector?
[02:42] Carlos: Yes, streaming works end-to-end. The adaptor proxies streaming connections and maintains a websocket or HTTP chunked response for the client. There are edge cases with load balancers but we document recommended LB configs.
[02:51] Aria: Security — SOC2, SSO, RBAC. We need to know what you can provide since our enterprise customers will ask.
[02:57] Maya: We're SOC2 Type II. We support SSO via SAML/OIDC and fine-grained RBAC in the console. For private deployments we can integrate with your IdP. We'll send our compliance pack after the call.
[03:08] Priya: Can you share a redacted SOC2 and pen test summary?
[03:11] Maya: Yes — action item there.
[03:14] [00:03:15] Samir (BlueEcho) joins: Sorry for the delay. Had run-over.
[03:17] Samir: Hi all, catching up — Aria, brief me on the scope.
[03:20] Aria: We're exploring integrating Redwood so BlueEcho customers can leverage Redwood models via our managed GPU offering — basically we present Redwood as a hosted model endpoint inside BlueEcho's console. Need to understand data residency, keys, and the technical connector pattern.
[03:33] Samir: Key Q for us is network egress cost and whether model weights ever transit our network or if inference happens in your runtime.
[03:40] Carlos: In the hosted model weights stay in Redwood runtime; the connector only forwards request payloads. If we do a private deployment or on-prem we can deploy runtime into your tenancy so weights sit in your environment.
[03:50] Samir: That matches our expectation. Another perf Q: for multi-GPU sharded models, do you expect NVLink if we want to host ourselves?
[03:59] Carlos: For large context LLMs that need model parallelism we usually recommend NVLink/PCIe-enabled clusters. If you plan to host runtime yourself, we can advise on topology. For partner-managed endpoints we can also provide replicas across multiple GPUs with KV cache strategies to reduce cross-GPU chatter.
[04:15] Liam: Can you describe the onboarding flow? How many steps to get a basic Orbit connector working?
[04:20] Maya: Typical onboarding: 1) sign MSA/NDA, 2) exchange network access & keys, 3) deploy connector (lightweight container), 4) run sanity tests and small benchmark, 5) pilot with reserved capacity. Usually 2-6 weeks depending on approvals.
[04:33] Aria: Timeline wise we're targeting a Q3 pilot with 10 enterprise customers. Is that feasible?
[04:39] Maya: Feasible. We recommend starting with 2-3 internal customers for the pilot first, and we can allocate a small dedicated pool for predictable perf. Carlos can scope the pool size once Liam shares expected QPS and model sizes.
[04:52] Liam: We'll share expected QPS soon. We need also to know about monitoring hooks — can we pull per-request logs and traces into our observability stack?
[05:00] Carlos: Yes — we expose tracing hooks and per-route metrics. For private deployments you can host the telemetry collector inside your VPC; for hosted we push to your splunk/datadog via secure endpoints. We also include token-level cost breakdowns and latency histograms.
[05:12] Priya: Any gotchas for enterprise procurement? We have some customers who insist on data residency and on-prem options.
[05:18] Maya: We have Private offering (VPC/on-prem) for exactly that. That requires an enterprise contract and usually a site-prep checklist — network, KMS access, baseline SLAs. We'll provide the runbook.
[05:27] Aria: Ok. On the partner program commercial mechanics — do you do rev share or reseller?
[05:31] Maya: Both are possible. Rev share typically has a minimum committed volume for partners, reseller is simpler but offers less margin. We can share the two templates. Action item: we'll include commercial template.
[05:40] Samir: For the POC we'd like to run a short benchmark against a 3rd party provider (NimblaCloud) to compare latency and cost. Is that doable?
[05:47] Carlos: Yes. We'll need sample payloads and model selection. We can run basic token-per-second and P95 latency tests on H100 and an A100 quantized path. We'll also include caching/batching configs.
[05:58] Liam: About model catalog — does Redwood provide curated open models or do customers bring their own?
[06:03] Carlos: Both. We have a model catalog with open models and performance profiles, and you can bring custom models. For bring-your-own-model we support versioning, rollouts, and compatibility checks.
[06:12] Aria: Any prebuilt BlueEcho UI components or SDKs? We want to put simple "Redwood" as an option in our console, ideally a one-click connect.
[06:20] Maya: We have SDKs and a small JS widget for onboarding. For more embedded options we can share a reference integration. That would be part of the partner playbook.
[06:29] Priya: Let's talk about licensing of the adaptor — is that open source or proprietary?
[06:33] Carlos: The adaptor is provided under a permissive license for partners; production-grade connectors are covered under the partner agreement. We can open source a reference adaptor if that helps accelerate integration.
[06:41] Aria: Nice. A few nitty-gritty questions: audit logs retention, SSO provisioning and SCIM, and support SLAs.
[06:49] Maya: Audit logs retention is configurable; default 90 days for hosted, longer with enterprise add-on. We support SAML/SCIM provisioning. Support SLAs vary by tier — enterprise gets 24x7 with an assigned CSM.
[06:59] Samir: Will you sign a subprocessor addendum? Some of our customers ask for that.
[07:04] Maya: Yes we have standard subprocessor agreements. We'll include that in the compliance pack.
[07:09] [00:07:10] Pause and quick screen share notes (links referenced):
- Partner spec draft (link): https://redwood.example.com/partners/blueecho/spec-draft
- Connector repo (reference): https://github.com/redwoodinc/connector-ref
- Compliance pack link: redwood.example.com/compliance/pack-redacted

[00:07:35] Carlos: If you want, we can run a small internal test in our lab: run a canonical prompt set, test P95, tokens/sec across A100/H100. That'd give numbers to compare with other providers.
[07:43] Priya: That would be super helpful for our GTM materials.
[07:46] Liam: On the routing side, how do we guarantee data locality per customer? Some customers must keep their data in eu-west only.
[07:54] Carlos: We support region constraints. You can pin models/routes to regions and the control plane will honor region-first placement. For hard guarantees, private deployment in the region is the safest; hosted can do region selection but not absolute physical isolation.
[08:06] Aria: Ok. Anything else we should know about maintenance windows and upgrade strategy?
[08:11] Maya: We schedule maintenance with advance notice; for Dedicated we have maintenance windows that avoid peak hours. For Private deployments upgrades are coordinated and can be pinned.
[08:20] Samir: For POC success criteria — what should we measure?
[08:24] Carlos: For a partner POC we recommend: 1) Latency P95 under agreed threshold (example <350ms), 2) Token cost per request within target band, 3) Functional parity vs existing provider (model output quality), and 4) Successful end-to-end onboarding inside BlueEcho console.
[08:42] Priya: We'll tailor that. We do have a couple of enterprise customers who require FIPS endpoints — do you support FIPS?
[08:49] Carlos: We have FIPS-compatible builds for private deployments. We'll confirm exact versions in the compliance pack.
[08:56] Aria: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[08:59] Maya: Recap for Redwood: 1) share partner integration spec + infra diagram (I'll send today), 2) send SOC2/attestation and subprocessor addendum links, 3) propose a benchmarking plan and suggested pool sizes after Liam provides QPS and model types.
[09:16] Aria: From BlueEcho: we'll send preferred GPU SKUs and initial list of pilot customers. Priya will capture commercial preferences.
[09:25] Maya: Cool. Shall we lock a follow-up technical DEEP dive week of 5/24?
[09:30] Liam: Works for me.
[09:31] Samir: Works.
[09:33] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with materials and a calendar invite.
[09:39] Aria: Thanks folks.
[09:40] End of meeting.
